title: Divide an Array Into Subarrays With Minimum Cost I
statement: Define the cost of a non-empty array as the value at its front, so `[3, 4, 1]` costs `3`. Cut `nums` into exactly three non-empty, contiguous, non-overlapping pieces that together use every element, and return the smallest possible sum of the three pieces' costs.
notes:
## Intuition

The first piece always starts at index 0, so `nums[0]` is always paid. The other two pieces start at two different later indices, and any two indices `1 <= i < j` can be chosen as starts. So the question is simply which two values after the first are the smallest. Trying every pair of cut points works too, but sorting the tail makes the choice obvious.

## Approach

1. Copy every value after the first into `rest` and sort it ascending.
2. Start `total` at `nums[0]`; it is the cost of the first piece no matter how we cut.
3. Scan the first two entries of `rest` and add each to `total`: they become the starts of the second and third pieces (the one with the smaller index goes second).
4. Return `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3, 12]`, so `rest = [2, 3, 12]`, already sorted, and `total` starts at `1`. The scan adds `rest[0] = 2` (total `3`) and `rest[1] = 3` (total `6`). That matches the pieces `[1]`, `[2]`, `[3, 12]`, so the answer is `6`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for sorting the tail (a single scan for the two minimums would be O(n)).
- Space: O(n) for the copy `rest`.

## Pitfalls

- `nums[0]` must always be counted; do not sort the whole array, or a small value could be "moved" to the front.
- Sorting numbers in JavaScript needs a comparator; the default sort compares strings, so `10` would come before `9`.
- The order of the two chosen starts does not matter, since any two later indices form valid cuts.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rest` | every value after the first, sorted ascending |
| `total` | running cost: the first value plus the starts chosen so far |
| `i` | which of the two cheapest starts is being added |

narration.2: Copy every value after the first; any two of them can start the other two pieces.
narration.3: Sort the copy so the cheapest starts come first.
narration.4: The first piece always begins at index 0, so its cost is always paid.
narration.5: Scan just the two smallest values of the sorted tail.
narration.6: Add one of the two cheapest starts to the total.
narration.8: Return the first value plus the two cheapest starts.
